The Sicklefin chub reaches a maximum total length of 11 centimeters [Li = 11 centimeters], a modest size consistent with other small-bodied cyprinids inhabiting the turbulent Great Plains rivers of North America. Field surveys conducted across the lower Missouri River system indicate that most individuals attain this ultimate length within two to three growing seasons, with growth rates strongly influenced by seasonal temperature regimes and prey availability. During the early developmental period, newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge at an exceptionally small size, with the wet weight at birth measuring a mere 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams]. This diminutive neonatal mass, derived from an egg diameter of approximately 0.7 millimeters, reflects the characteristics of a pelagic spawning strategy typical of riverine cyprinids that produce numerous small, semi-buoyant ova. The substantial investment in fecundity rather than individual offspring mass is an adaptation to the high levels of egg and larval mortality inherent in their dynamic, sand-bed river habitats.

Sexual maturation in the Sicklefin chub occurs at a distinct morphological landmark. Individuals typically attain puberty once they reach a total length of approximately 7 centimeters [Lp = approximately 7 centimeters], a threshold that has been confirmed through histological examination of gonadal tissue in specimens collected from the Mississippi River basin. At this stage of development, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is estimated at 3.4 grams [Wwp = 3.4 grams], representing a substantial increase from the minute birth mass. The transition to reproductive maturity is accompanied by the onset of vitellogenesis in females and the initiation of spermatogenesis in males, marking a critical shift in energetic allocation from somatic growth toward reproductive potential. This length-based rather than strictly age-based maturation schedule allows individuals to capitalize on favorable growing conditions; during years of abundant food resources, some fast-growing young-of-year may approach or even reach the 7-centimeter threshold before their first winter.

Under a constant water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], researchers have recorded a lifespan of approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] for this species. This longevity is relatively extended for a small-bodied cyprinid and may be linked to the species' low metabolic demands and the comparatively stable thermal environment of the deeper river channels it occupies. The maximum recorded lifespan of 5 years [am = 5 years] contrasts with the shorter life expectancies observed in some more diminutive minnow species of the same region, suggesting that the Sicklefin chub follows a somewhat slower life-history pace at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. In the wild, however, few individuals likely reach this physiological maximum due to the combined pressures of predation from piscivorous fishes, fluctuating flow regimes that can scour spawning habitat, and the energetic costs of repeated spawning events across multiple seasons. The incubation temperature used in these laboratory studies closely approximates the summer thermal maxima frequently recorded in the species' native range.

At the same constant temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the time since birth at puberty for the Sicklefin chub has been determined to be approximately 92 days since birth [tp = approximately 92 days since birth]. This relatively rapid progression from hatching to the onset of gonadal development is notable among Great Plains cyprinids and reflects a life-history strategy geared toward early maturation in a hydrologically unpredictable environment. The combination of a short pre-pubertal period and a moderate lifespan of 5 years [am = 5 years] indicates that reproductive opportunities are concentrated within a relatively narrow window following the attainment of the 7-centimeter (7 centimeters) [Lp = 7 centimeters] length threshold at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. The developmental timeline of 92 days since birth [tp = 92 days since birth] is supported by growth trajectory analyses from otolith microchemistry studies, which show a rapid linear increase in body size during the first three months of life when water temperatures remain elevated at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. Juveniles that fail to accumulate sufficient somatic reserves during this critical early period may experience a delayed onset of maturity.

The ultimate wet weight of the Sicklefin chub has been calculated at 13.7 grams [Wwi = 13.7 grams], representing the theorized asymptotic body mass that adults approach as they complete their somatic growth trajectory. This value, derived from length-weight regressions based on the 7-centimeter (7 centimeters) [Lp = 7 centimeters] length at puberty, suggests that post-maturation growth is comparatively modest in this species. Gravid females nearing the ultimate total length of 11 centimeters [Li = 11 centimeters] often approach the upper mass limit of 13.7 grams [Wwi = 13.7 grams], although individual variation is considerable and influenced by local prey abundance and interannual flow conditions. The relatively small energetic surplus allocated to post-pubertal somatic expansion, combined with the early maturation schedule of 92 days since birth [tp = 92 days since birth] at 21 °C, underscores a life-history strategy prioritizing rapid initial growth and early reproductive output over continued asymptotic size increase at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This pattern aligns with that observed in other pelagic-broadcast spawning cyprinids adapted to the seasonally dynamic environments of the North American Great Plains.
